# BCD store generated by winbootfix (level c, experimental)

When `EFI\Microsoft\Boot\BCD` is missing, unreadable, or points to a partition that no longer exists
(typical after cloning a disk), winbootfix writes a new store from
`<Windows>\System32\config\BCD-Template`, reproducing what `bcdboot <win> /s <esp> /f UEFI` does on a GPT
disk. The code is in [`src/winbootfix/boot/bcd/`](../src/winbootfix/boot/bcd/).

## Why "experimental"

The BCD format is not documented as a file format by Microsoft. The registry layout and element types below
are those of Microsoft's BCD WMI provider documentation (`BcdLibraryElementTypes`,
`BcdBootMgrElementTypes`, `BcdOSLoaderElementTypes`, `BcdResumeElementTypes`); the binary encoding of
"device" elements comes from reverse engineering of stores written by `bcdboot`. Therefore:

1. the generated store is re-read and checked before being installed (`validate.check`): Boot Manager
   device = EFI partition, default entry = an OS loader whose `device` and `osdevice` are the Windows
   partition, `path` = `\Windows\system32\winload.efi`, `systemroot` = `\Windows`;
2. the post-repair script runs `bcdboot` from Windows at the first start and replaces the store with an
   official one (the previous store is kept as `BCD.winbootfix` until bcdboot succeeds);
3. if the store cannot be built or checked, winbootfix says so and recommends the WinPE variant
   (`bcdboot` from Microsoft's own environment);
4. the VM test scenario `tests/vm/scenarios/bcd.sh` deletes the store of a real Windows and checks that
   Windows starts with the generated one.

## Registry layout

A BCD store is a registry hive:

```
Description\KeyName = "BCD00000000" (REG_SZ), System = 1, TreatAsSystem = 1 (REG_DWORD)
Objects\{object GUID}\Description\Type             REG_DWORD   object type
Objects\{object GUID}\Elements\<type, 8 hex>\Element  value      element value
```

Value type by element format (bits 24-27 of the element type):

| Format | Registry type | Encoding |
|---|---|---|
| 1 device | REG_BINARY | see below |
| 2 string | REG_SZ | UTF-16LE |
| 3 object | REG_SZ | `{guid}` |
| 4 object list | REG_MULTI_SZ | `{guid}` list |
| 5 integer | REG_BINARY | 8 bytes little-endian |
| 6 boolean | REG_BINARY | 1 byte |
| 7 integer list | REG_BINARY | n × 8 bytes |

## Objects written

| Object | GUID | Type | Elements |
|---|---|---|---|
| Windows Boot Manager | `{9dea862c-5cdd-4e70-acc1-f32b344d4795}` | `0x10100002` | `11000001` device = ESP · `12000002` path = `\EFI\Microsoft\Boot\bootmgfw.efi` · `12000004` "Windows Boot Manager" · `12000005` locale · `14000006` inherit `{globalsettings}` · `23000003` default = loader · `23000006` resume object · `24000001` display order = [loader] · `24000010` tools = [`{memdiag}`] · `25000004` timeout = 30 |
| Windows Boot Loader | new GUID | `0x10200003` | `11000001` device = Windows partition · `12000002` `\Windows\system32\winload.efi` · `12000004` "Windows 10" / "Windows 11" · `12000005` locale · `14000006` inherit `{bootloadersettings}` · `16000060` isolated context = true · `17000077` allowed in-memory settings = [`0x15000075`] · `21000001` osdevice = Windows partition · `22000002` systemroot = `\Windows` · `23000003` resume object · `25000020` nx = OptIn (0) · `250000c2` boot menu policy = Standard (1) |
| Resume from Hibernate | new GUID | `0x10200004` | `11000001` device · `12000002` `\Windows\system32\winresume.efi` · `12000004` · `12000005` · `14000006` inherit `{resumeloadersettings}` · `16000060` · `17000077` · `21000001` file device · `22000002` file path = `\hiberfil.sys` |
| Memory Diagnostic | `{b2721d73-1db4-4c62-bf78-c548a880142d}` | `0x10200005` | `11000001` device = ESP · `12000002` `\EFI\Microsoft\Boot\memtest.efi` · `12000004` · `12000005` · `14000006` inherit `{globalsettings}` |

Inherited settings objects (`{globalsettings}` `{7ea2e1ac-…}`, `{bootloadersettings}` `{6efb52bf-…}`,
`{resumeloadersettings}` `{1afa9c49-…}`, `{dbgsettings}`, `{emssettings}`, `{badmemory}`,
`{hypervisorsettings}`) normally come from the template; missing ones are created with their type and their
inheritance list only. The locale is the Windows UI language (e.g. `fr-FR`).

## Device element (88 bytes), partition on a GPT disk

| Offset | Size | Content |
|---|---|---|
| 0x00 | 16 | additional options GUID (zero) |
| 0x10 | 4 | device type: 6 = partition |
| 0x14 | 4 | flags (0) |
| 0x18 | 4 | size of the data from 0x10: 0x48 |
| 0x1C | 4 | reserved (0) |
| 0x20 | 16 | partition unique GUID (GPT `PARTUUID`, mixed-endian `bytes_le`) |
| 0x30 | 4 | partition style: 0 = GPT (1 = MBR) |
| 0x34 | 4 | reserved |
| 0x38 | 16 | disk GUID (GPT `PTUUID`, `bytes_le`) |
| 0x48 | 16 | zero padding |

For MBR disks, 0x20 holds the partition byte offset (u64) and 0x38 the 32-bit disk signature; winbootfix
decodes this form for diagnosis but does not write MBR stores (Legacy mode is not supported).

## Diagnosis of an existing store

`validate.read` decodes `{bootmgr}`, the default entry, its devices, path and system root.
`validate.check` reports `unreadable`, `no_bootmgr`, `no_default`, `default_missing`,
`default_not_osloader`, `bootmgr_device_mismatch`, `device_mismatch`, `osdevice_mismatch`,
`path_mismatch`, `systemroot_mismatch`, or `device_unverifiable` when a device uses another encoding
(for example `locate` or `boot`). Only the serious problems trigger a rebuild; an unverifiable store is
reported but left alone.
